The European Commission is proposing to turn an existing EU rulebook, the Settlement Finality Directive (SFD), into a Regulation. A directive leaves each country to put its rules into national law, while a regulation applies the same rules directly across the EU. The aim is to make the rules more uniform and to update them for new technology.

The SFD was adopted in 1998 to reduce risk in the systems that process payments and transfer securities. Its key protection is that once a transfer order has entered a designated system, it cannot be undone, even if a participant becomes insolvent. The directive has been amended six times since then. A 2021 public consultation and a 2023 Commission report found that member states had applied its obligations differently. These differences fragment the single market, create legal uncertainty, and make it harder for firms to trade and invest across borders.

The proposal sets out the rules more precisely in several areas: legal certainty for digital innovation, conflict-of-law rules, participation of EU entities in systems based outside the EU, who may take part, which securities are covered, how EU systems are designated, transparency, and the moments at which settlement becomes final. It is also meant to be technology-neutral, so that new tools such as distributed ledger technology can be used while their risks are still managed. The proposal fits within broader EU goals of building a Capital Markets Union and a Savings and Investments Union.

The budgetary figures are indicative, because the proposal depends on the EU's multiannual budget for 2028 to 2034, which has not yet been finally adopted.
